title: Robin's Unexpected Garden Party
markdown:
The Grand Conservatory had been washed and waiting since dawn. Orchids breathed their sweet, expensive perfume into the glassed air, and every dewdrop on every rose had, in Robin’s private ledger, a lineage. He was a weasel of wire spectacles and garden history, a creature who believed careful planning was not the enemy of joy but its most elegant architect. He smoothed his waistcoat, tested the seating cards with a paw, and found the alignment satisfactory to the width of a whisker.

“Bea,” he said, voice a soft rustle. “The seating. Unequivocally precise?”

Bea the goat, his flatmate and a creature of hay-scented practicality, had a stubborn vine around one horn. “Precisely as you drew it. Though this begonia is wondering if it should have been a fern.”

Robin’s whiskers gave the faintest tremor. Deviation, even botanical, sat badly with him. “Existential crises are for philosophers, not prize-winning begonias. The programmes. Silk ribbon. Instruction twenty-seven, subsection B.”

Bea trotted over with a stack under one arm. “Tied as requested. They would rather dance.” A single programme, with a flourish of defiance, slid to the polished floor. “See?”

He stooped, straightened the card as if it were a wounded bird, and told himself they were not losing control. They were broadening the interpretation. The antique garden clock chimed, melodious and a little melancholy. “Grace under pressure,” he advised.

Bea butted his shoulder, gentle. “My middle name. Actually it is Agnes, but you have the idea.”

The Ornithological Society arrived first, hushed as a hide. Mr Finch, their chairman, took Robin’s paw in both of his. “Mr Nightingale. Honoured. The native flora promises a stimulating evening. We hope to note anything that might tempt a lesser-spotted woodpecker.”

“Nightingale? I am Robin. Robin Weasel. The garden historian.”

The second party burst in on a clink of teacups. Mrs Gable clapped his shoulder hard enough to unsettle a button. “Robin, darling. Literature and this enchanting setting. Are the canapés ready? I am famished for a cucumber sandwich.”

Before he could sort Nightingale from Gable from himself, the Aromatherapy Enthusiasts drifted through the doors in a cloud of lavender and chamomile. Willow, their serene captain, inclined her head as if the conservatory were a chapel. “Peace. We understand there is a presentation on the therapeutic properties of rare blooms. I have brought my finest diffusers.”

Three societies. Each certain it was the sole honoured guest. Robin felt the glass roof tilt. He might have burrowed under a robust fern until Monday and left the orchids to explain themselves. Bea, meaning to help, nudged a table of seed packets and sent rare seeds skating across the floor like a second, smaller disaster.

He looked at the expectant faces: binoculars, novels, diffusers. He looked at the unruly programmes. He breathed orchids, damp earth, and a hint of Bea’s hay. The wood was cool under his paws. Somewhere beyond the glass a bird tried a phrase and thought better of it.

“Well,” he said, and his voice surprised him by holding. “It appears we have an eclectic gathering. And the programmes are offering a robust interpretation of stiff.”

Mr Finch peered at Mrs Gable. “Are you a contributor to Avian Wonders?”

“Heavens no. I write about tension in Victorian novels. Your binoculars, though. For birds, or for distant literary critiques?”

Willow opened her eyes. “The energy is multifaceted. Many intentions, one room.”

Robin found a wryness that was almost courage. “Our administrative assistant,” he said, and winked at Bea, who was polishing a terracotta pot with her tail, “has invited a fascinating mix. The original programme concerned the historical significance of the Dodo Feather Orchid.” He indicated a bloom whose petals had never agreed on a colour. “Tonight we shall have a symposium.”

He and Bea, chaotic and willing, began to braid the evening. He showed the ornithologists how a finch’s nesting turn had once been copied into textile borders, the sort of quiet theft that pleased both stitchers and birds. He told the book club how botanical plates in early chapbooks had taught people to imagine jungles they would never walk, and Mrs Gable made a note as if a novel had just grown a greenhouse. A flask of essential oil tipped—Bea’s elbow, or the flask’s own idea—and the Dodo Feather Orchid answered with an uplifting scent Willow declared a fortunate accident. Guests drifted from group to group. A woodpecker was discussed as a character. A Victorian heroine was accused of smelling faintly of chamomile. The seating plan, so carefully drawn, became a suggestion the chairs ignored.

Later a tall stack of programmes, ribbons loosened by conversation and heat, leaned toward a crash. Robin caught it with a practised paw instead of a panic. Bea nudged him. “Dignity is not stiffness. It is knowing when the programmes may dance.”

He set the stack down crooked on purpose and left it so.

When the last guest left, faces unexpectedly bright, the conservatory was dishevelled and harmonious. Cucumber crumbs marked a trail the woodpecker would have enjoyed. A diffuser still breathed lavender in a corner as if the night had not quite finished thinking. The programmes lay askew on a table like dancers after a ball.

“More fun than a purely planned event,” Bea said, stretching until her bells of horn caught the last lamp. “More organic.”

Robin’s whiskers were still. He did not announce that joy had been architected. He only looked at the orchids, which had managed, without instruction twenty-seven, to be beautiful; at the seeds on the floor, which would have to be gathered in the morning; and at Bea, whose middle name was Agnes and whose talent was for remaining.

“Indeed,” he said. “Indeed it was.”
